item.title: Bronze Medalist
item.description: Tonga has ended a 16-year Commonwealth Games medal drought after heavyweight judoka Paula Monta claimed a historic bronze medal in the men's +100kg competition at the Glasgow 2026 Commonwealth Games. Paula Monta became Tonga's first and only medalist of the Commonwelath Games since 2010 after defeating Canada's John Messe Bessong in a hard-fought bronze medal contest.
item.content:encoded:
Tonga has ended a 16-year Commonwealth Games medal drought after heavyweight judoka Paula Monta claimed a historic bronze medal in the men's +100kg competition at the Glasgow 2026 Commonwealth Games.

Paula Monta became Tonga's first and only medalist of the Commonwelath Games since 2010 after defeating Canada's John Messe Bessong in a hard-fought bronze medal contest.

The encounter went the full distance, with Monta holding off a late challenge from the Canadian Judoka to secure victory by the narrowest of margins. He prevailed with one waza-ari and two yuko to Bessong's one waza-ari and one yuko.

The bronze medal is a remarkable campaign for the 21-year-old, who fought his way through the repechage after an earlier defeat to earn another chance at the podium before delivering under pressure in the medal playoff.

The result ends the nation's 16-year wait for a Commonwealth Games medal and providing Team Tonga with its first podium finish of the Glasgow Games.

Monta's success follows months of preparation in Japan under the guidance of coach Josateki Naulu, the former Fiji international judoka and Olympian. The Tonga Judo Association credited Naulu's dedication and expertise as instrumental in preparing Monta for the historic performance.

In recognition of his achievement, Monta was also named Tonga's flag bearer for Team Tonga in the Commonwealth Games closing ceremony.

The Glasgow 2026 Commonwealth Games officially concluded on Sunday, August 2, 2026, with a vibrant closing ceremony inside the OVO Hydro arena in Glasgow, Scotland. The 11-day sporting event wrapped up with musical performances, athlete parades, and the formal handover of the Commonwealth Games flag to the next host city.

Amdavad (Ahmedabad), India, will host the Centenary Games in 2030.

item.content:encoded:
The Legislative Assembly of Tonga, on reconvening this morning, 3 August, unseated two Members of Parliament, Semisi Sika (former Minister for Infrastructure and Minister for Tourism/Tongatapu 2) and Lataifaingata’a Tangimana (former Minister for Finance/Niua 17).

The Courts determined the unseating, after the two MP s failed in their appeals against the certification of offences of bribery under the Electoral Act in the lead up to the November 2025 General Election.

The Speaker of Parliament Lord Vaea received the Certificate of Determination from the Court of Appeal, in accordance with Clauses 32 and 37 of the Electoral Act.

In total, five election petitions were filed with the Court, following the November 2025 General Election, concerning Tongatapu 2, Tongatapu 9, ʻEua 11, Vavaʻu 16, and Niua 17.

The Speaker announced that Lataifaingata’a Tangimana (Niua 17) had resigned his seat on 31 July.

Pursuant to Clause 74 of the Constitution of Tonga, the Speaker noted that an unseating motion was unnecessary for Tangimana as his seat was already vacant.

This raised concerns from several members of the House.

Piveni Piukala, the Tongatapu No. 7 People’s Representative, was concerned because the law states that if a member is unseated, that member will be unable to run for Parliament for the next five years. If the House recognised that the member had resigned, he questioned whether iit would contradict the law.

The Speaker responded that the seat became vacant on the day the member resigned.

Deputy PM Hon. Dr Viliami Latu noted that Clause 40 of the Electoral Act had already disqualified that person from being nominated as a candidate in any election held within five years of the date on which his election was declared void.

Piveni Piukala remained concerned about the clarity of the law.

The PM , Lord Fakafanua, said that Clauses 66 and 76 of the Constitution have contradictions and that the decision would have to be made by the Speaker of the House.

Piveni Piukala argued that Clause 76 specifically required the House to unseat the member.

The Minister for Health Hon. Huʻakavameiliku argued that the member had the right to resign.

The Speaker reminded members that the decision to unseat had already been made. He warned the House that the unseating was made to respect the decision of the Court.

The PM proposed that the member be unseated effective from 30 July, the date the Court delivered its ruling. He said the House could make that decision.

The Speaker said the effective date would be today, 3 August, when the House resumed its work.

Mateni Tapueluelu, the Tongatapu No. 4 People’s Representative, wanted the Speaker to read the letter from Tangimana. He was concerned about the former member continuing to receive parliamentary privileges, including his salary, after the Court had declared his election void.

The Speaker was disappointed by the issues raised by members. “You are not abiding by the rules, and I am concerned that you do not respect them.”

The Speaker told members they were questioning the judgments of the Court and urged the House to respect the Court.

The Speaker noted that both members were unseated today, and to be recorded as such in the parliamentary minutes.

item.title: Aid to the Pacific region is increasingly debt-driven
item.description: Official Development Finance to the Pacific increased in 2024 reaching US $4.1 billion, ending three years of decline, but a new report says the rise came predominantly from concessional loans, which offset falling year-on-year grants. The Pacific aid landscape has stabilised but is increasingly debt-driven, says the Lowy Institute in a new report published today.
item.content:encoded:
Official Development Finance to the Pacific increased in 2024 reaching US $4.1 billion, ending three years of decline, but a new report says the rise came predominantly from concessional loans, which offset falling year-on-year grants.

The Pacific aid landscape has stabilised but is increasingly debt-driven, says the Lowy Institute in a new report published today.

The ’Pacific Aid Map 2026’ which tracks aid and development finance flows across the Pacific, notes that Australia remains the largest Pacific Aid partner.

Riley Duke, researcher at the Lowy Institute, said the 2026 version of the interactive map https://pacificaidmap.lowyinstitute.org/ was published today.

“This year we added a currency change tool, so all the data can be viewed in different Pacific currencies, including Tongan paʻanga.”

Australia largest Pacific aid partner Aid to the Pacific is increasingly concentrated among a few major partners, with Australia by far the largest. The United States has cemented a long-term but narrow commitment to the three Compact states.

Australia and multilateral development banks dominate lending to the region. • Australia has signed US $2.4 billion in new loan agreements since 2021. • Strategic infrastructure – ports, airports, telecommunications, and power generation – has accounted for more than half of all new infrastructure commitments since 2020, and infrastructure overall has risen from 15% of regional development finance in 2008 to more than a third by 2019.

The Lowy Institute reported that China maintains aid strategy shift from large-scale lending to high-frequency, small-scale grants. China's Pacific aid remains below its 2010s peak but has stabilised around a high-visibility grant model tied to diplomatic objectives. Loans from its mid-2010s lending boom are now entering acute repayment phases.

” Chinese state-owned firms dominate Pacific infrastructure contracts. Chinese state-owned enterprises have become the dominant construction contractors for Pacific infrastructure, including on projects financed by multilateral development banks. This position has held even as Beijing's own direct financing has declined.

“Chinese SOE s have been involved in more than US $5.1 billion of Pacific infrastructure since 2008, around US $3 billion financed directly by China and the rest by the ADB and World Bank, accounting for roughly 40% of Pacific infrastructure projects by value.”

The Lowy Institute said that the Iran war is the latest in a series of shocks to hit the region, but the scale of the international response is uncertain. Pacific economies have limited capacity to absorb shocks such as the Iran war, leaving them at risk of a "lost decade" of development on top of earlier crises.

Energy insecurity persists despite renewables focus. Pacific Island economies are among the world's most energy insecure. Recent fuel-market volatility has underscored continued dependence on imported fossil fuels despite sustained investment in renewables.

The Lowy Institute is an independent, nonpartisan international policy think tank. The Institute provides high-quality research and distinctive perspectives on the issues and trends shaping Australia’s role in the world. The Pacific Aid Map is now in its ninth year, covering 50,000+ projects and $60 billion in finance since 2008, and it's the most detailed picture available of who's funding what in the region.
